title: Reentrancy in StakingVault.withdraw() allows draining funds
summary: The staking vault sent a user their money before recording that they had withdrawn it. A malicious contract could exploit that gap to call withdraw again and again in a single transaction, draining every user's deposit at once.
description: `withdraw()` performs the external ETH transfer before zeroing the caller's balance, violating Checks-Effects-Interactions. A contract with a re-entrant `receive()` recursively re-enters `withdraw()` before the balance update, withdrawing repeatedly.
impact: Complete loss of all funds held by the vault in a single transaction — the most severe possible outcome for a DeFi protocol. A Foundry PoC drained the full test balance.
stepsToReproduce: Deploy an attacker contract that deposits a small amount
Call withdraw() once; it re-enters until the vault is empty

evidence.title: Vulnerable withdraw (Checks-Effects-Interactions violated)
Attacker contract
PoC drain (testnet)
evidence.description: Foundry test draining the vault's entire 50 ETH test balance in one tx.

remediation.recommendation: Apply Checks-Effects-Interactions: update `balances` before the external call, and add a `nonReentrant` guard (OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard).
remediation.verification: Re-ran the exploit suite; drain no longer possible. Added an invariant test asserting total balances == contract balance.

title: Missing access control on setRewardRate()
summary: A function that controls how many rewards the protocol pays out had no owner check, so anyone could call it and set the reward rate to whatever they wanted — draining the reward pool.
description: `setRewardRate()` lacked an `onlyOwner` modifier. Any address could set an arbitrary reward rate, enabling economic abuse and reward-pool drain.
impact: Unauthorized control of protocol economics; an attacker could inflate rewards to themselves and drain the distributor.

evidence.title: Unprotected privileged function

remediation.recommendation: Add an access-control modifier (onlyOwner or role-based). Prefer multi-sig ownership and a timelock for economic parameters.

title: Uninitialized UUPS proxy can be hijacked
summary: The upgradeable token's implementation contract was left un-initialised, so an attacker could claim ownership of the implementation and, via the upgrade mechanism, potentially take control of the token.
description: The implementation contract behind the UUPS proxy did not disable initializers in its constructor. An attacker can call `initialize()` on the implementation and become owner, then abuse `upgradeTo` semantics.
impact: Potential takeover of the token's upgrade authority, which could lead to malicious upgrades affecting all holders.

remediation.recommendation: Call `_disableInitializers()` in the implementation constructor; restrict `initialize` to once; guard `_authorizeUpgrade` with owner/role checks and a timelock.

title: Internal admin panel served over cleartext HTTP
summary: An internal admin tool sent its login and data over plain, unencrypted HTTP. Anyone on the office network could read the credentials straight off the wire.
description: Traffic capture on the corporate segment showed the admin panel authenticating over HTTP. Credentials and session tokens were visible in plaintext.
impact: Any attacker with network access (rogue device, compromised host, malicious insider) could capture admin credentials and sessions.

evidence.title: Captured cleartext login
evidence.content:
POST /admin/login HTTP/1.1
Host: admin.internal
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=ops&password=Spr1ng2026!

evidence.title: Wireshark capture
evidence.description: HTTP POST with plaintext credentials observed on the corporate segment.

remediation.recommendation: Serve all internal apps over HTTPS with valid certs and HSTS; redirect HTTP→HTTPS; disable plaintext protocols; rotate exposed credentials.

title: Flat network segment reaches production database
summary: The office network can reach the production database directly, with no segmentation in between. If any office machine is compromised, the attacker is one hop from the crown-jewel data.
description: Flow-log and scan analysis showed the corporate VLAN can open connections to the production PostgreSQL port. There is no network segmentation or bastion enforcing separation.
impact: A single compromised laptop provides a direct path to the production database, dramatically shortening the attack chain to sensitive data.

remediation.recommendation: Segment corporate and production networks; require a bastion/VPN with MFA for DB access; restrict DB security groups to app subnets; add east-west monitoring.

title: API connection pool exhausts at ~500 concurrent users
summary: Load testing showed that above about 500 people using the service at once, the database connections run out and the whole API starts timing out for everyone — an availability risk that an attacker could trigger deliberately.
description: k6 tests showed p99 latency climbing sharply past ~500 concurrent users as the fixed database connection pool saturated. Beyond the breaking point, healthy requests failed alongside the load and the service required manual recovery.
impact: Total service outage under peak or malicious load; a low-effort denial-of-service condition and a real risk during traffic spikes (launches, campaigns).
stepsToReproduce: Run k6 ramp to 800 VUs against /api
Observe connection pool at 100% and cascading 503s

evidence.title: k6 summary at breaking point
evidence.content:
running (5m00s), 800/800 VUs
  http_req_duration.....: p(95)=6.9s p(99)=8.4s
  http_req_failed.......: 41.2% ✓ 0 ✗ 33021
  db_pool_wait..........: avg=4.1s max=12.0s  # pool saturated

remediation.recommendation: Add horizontal autoscaling, bound and tune the DB connection pool with backpressure, add per-client rate limiting, and implement graceful degradation / load shedding. Define SLOs and alerts.
remediation.verification: Re-tested to 1,500 VUs with autoscaling + bounded pools; p99 stayed under 1.5s with no cascading failures.
